title: Athena: Spear and Loom
summary: A lunar month with Athena: her birth from the head of Zeus, the craft goddess of weaving and work, the warrior of strategy and defence, the city goddess of the Panathenaia, and how to honour her with olive oil, skilled work and fair counsel.
welcome:
This is a month of study and devotion with Athena, the Greek goddess of skilled work and clever counsel, of weaving and pottery, of strategy and the defence of the city. She is often reduced to “the goddess of wisdom.” The Greeks saw her as something more practical and more formidable: the one who teaches craftspeople their skills, stands beside heroes in danger and keeps the city safe.

It is a self-dedication, not an initiation. No priesthood stands behind it, and it does not replace any group’s initiation. Ancient Athenians honoured many gods along with her, and you can too.

You will need olive oil, a bowl of water, a project you are working on, whether a craft, a course of study, or work you care about, and the patience to do it well.
about: Athena sprang fully armed from the head of Zeus, after he had swallowed her mother Metis, whose name means cunning intelligence. She was Pallas, Parthenos the maiden, Glaukopis the bright-eyed, and the patron of Athens, which she won from Poseidon by giving it the olive tree. She was Ergane, the worker, who taught weaving to women and crafts to men: the loom, the potter’s wheel, the chariot, the ship. She was Promachos, who fights in the front line, but her war is strategy and defence, not the frenzy of Ares. She guided Odysseus and Perseus and, in Aeschylus’ Eumenides, founded the court that judged Orestes. Athens honoured her at the Panathenaia every summer with a newly woven robe, and on the third of each month. Rome knew her as Minerva. Today Hellenic polytheists honour her with olive oil, olives, honey cakes and finished work, and many people of every path see her as a patron of study, craft, justice and courage.
notes: Athena is a war goddess as well as a goddess of wisdom and craft. Her war is protection and strategy. This journey keeps devotional and protective work only.

The best-known modern version of Medusa’s story, in which Athena punishes her after she is raped in Athena’s temple, comes from the Roman poet Ovid. Earlier Greek sources tell it differently. The journey explains both.
Arachne’s story, too, is told fully only by Ovid. It is Roman, not Greek cult, though it is worth knowing.
Olive oil is her central offering. Burning oil lamps need care: never leave them unattended.

stages.title: An offering of oil
stages.intro: Athena gave Athens the olive, so the journey begins with olive oil: a clean shrine, washed hands, a drop of oil and an introduction. If you can, begin on the third day of the lunar month, counting the Noumenia, the first crescent, as day one: that was her monthly day.

practices.title: Choose your work
practices.instructions: Choose one piece of work you will bring to Athena this month: a craft project, something you are studying, a skill at your job, a problem you want to solve well. Set out its tools near where her shrine will be.
practices.prompt: What did you choose, and why that?

rite.title: Introduction with olive oil
rite.summary: Purify, begin with Hestia, greet Athena with incense and a libation of olive oil, and set your work before her.

ingredients.name: A bowl of fresh water and a match for khernips
A candle or small oil lamp
A little olive oil in a small cup
A tool or piece of the work you chose

rite.preparation: Clean and tidy the shrine place; Athena is a goddess of order and good work. Set out the candle, the water, the cup of oil and the dish, with the tool or work beside them. Wash and dress neatly.

steps.title: Make khernips
steps.instructions: Quench the match in the water, wash your hands and sprinkle a few drops on your face and on the work.

steps.title: Begin with Hestia
steps.instructions: Light the candle or lamp and let a drop of oil fall on the dish for Hestia.
steps.spoken: Hestia, first and last: I begin with you.

steps.title: Call Athena
steps.instructions: Light the incense if you have it. Stand straight, raise your hands, palms up.
steps.spoken: Pallas Athena, bright-eyed daughter of Zeus, Ergane the worker, Polias guardian of the city: I am [your name]. I bring you oil from the olive you gave, and this work of my hands. I have come to learn who you are. Look on my work and teach me.

steps.title: Pour the oil
steps.instructions: Pour most of the olive oil slowly into the dish. Touch the tool or work. Sit for a few minutes and think about what doing this work well would mean.

steps.title: Close with Hestia
steps.instructions: Let the last drop fall for Hestia, thank them both and put out the flame.
steps.spoken: Hestia, last as you were first. Athena, thank you.

rite.closing: Wipe the oil from the dish onto earth outside or onto a cloth to dispose of; do not pour oil down the sink. Leave the tool on the shrine overnight, then use it. Write down your work and what doing it well would look like.
rite.safety: Never leave a candle or oil lamp burning unattended; spilled oil near a flame catches quickly. Keep the shrine on a stable, heatproof surface. Use incense sparingly near pets and anyone with asthma.

stages.title: Learning the bright-eyed one
stages.intro: Ten days of reading: her birth and nature, her crafts, her war and justice, and how Athens honoured her.

lessons.title: Born from the head of Zeus
lessons.summary: Metis, the strange birth, and the goddess Aphrodite cannot bend.

sections.heading: Metis swallowed
sections.body:
Hesiod tells how Zeus’s first wife was Metis, a goddess whose name means cunning intelligence, practical cleverness. It was foretold that she would bear a son who would overthrow his father. So when she was pregnant, Zeus swallowed her, so that, as Hesiod says, she would advise him from within. In time, Athena was born from his head.

The story says something precise. Athena is the daughter of practical intelligence, and that intelligence lives on inside the king of the gods. Her wisdom is metis: knowing how to do things, how to get out of trouble, how to make and plan.

sections.heading: The armed birth
sections.body:
The Homeric hymn to Athena (number 28) describes the birth. “From his awful head wise Zeus himself bare her arrayed in warlike arms of flashing gold, and awe seized all the gods as they gazed.” Olympus reeled, the earth cried out, the sea boiled and the sun stopped his horses, “until the maiden Pallas Athene had stripped the heavenly armour from her immortal shoulders. And wise Zeus was glad.”

The same hymn calls her “bright-eyed, inventive, unbending of heart, pure virgin, saviour of cities, courageous, Tritogeneia.” Each word is a power. Tritogeneia is old and obscure; it may mean “born at Lake Triton” or “third-born,” and no one is sure.

sections.heading: The goddess Aphrodite cannot bend
sections.body:
The Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite names Athena first among the three goddesses Aphrodite cannot bend. “She has no pleasure in the deeds of golden Aphrodite, but delights in wars and in the work of Ares, in strifes and battles and in preparing famous crafts.” Then it adds: “She first taught earthly craftsmen to make chariots of war and cars variously wrought with bronze, and she, too, teaches tender maidens in the house and puts knowledge of goodly arts in each one’s mind.”

There you have both halves of her in a few lines: war and craft, the battlefield and the loom. For the Greeks these belonged together. Both need skill, planning and a steady hand.

sections.heading: Older roots
sections.body: A Linear B tablet from Knossos, from around 1400 BCE, mentions a-ta-na-po-ti-ni-ja, often read as “the Mistress of Atana,” which may be the oldest trace of her name, though it may refer to a place. Many scholars think Athena was originally the protecting goddess of a Bronze Age citadel, a palace goddess, and that her name and Athens’ name are linked. She was not only Athenian, though. Sparta, Argos, Troy and many other cities had their own Athenas.

knowAndDont.known: Hesiod’s Theogony (886–900, 924–926) tells of Metis and the head birth. Homeric Hymns XXVIII and V describe her nature. She was worshipped in many Greek cities as a citadel goddess.
knowAndDont.unknown: The meaning of Tritogeneia, and whether the Knossos tablet refers to Athena, are uncertain. Her origins as a Bronze Age palace goddess are a strong theory, not a proven fact.

lessons.inPractice: Many devotees keep an owl image, an olive branch or a small helmet on her shrine, and begin study or planning with a moment of quiet asking for metis, clear practical thinking.
reflect: Where in your life do you use metis, practical cunning?
War and craft together: does that pairing make sense to you?
further: Hesiod, Theogony 886–926, trans. H. G. Evelyn-White (1914)
Homeric Hymn XXVIII to Athena, trans. H. G. Evelyn-White (1914)

lessons.title: Ergane: the worker
lessons.summary: Weaving, pottery and the crafts of Athena, the Panathenaic robe, and Arachne.

sections.heading: Goddess of craftspeople
sections.body:
Athena Ergane, “the worker,” was the goddess of skilled hands. She was credited with inventing or teaching weaving, spinning, pottery, carpentry, the building of the first ship (the Argo), the bridle for horses (as Athena Hippia), the chariot and the trumpet. Potters painted her on their vases and dedicated pots to her; carpenters and smiths honoured her with Hephaistos, the god of the forge.

At the Chalkeia, a festival of bronze-smiths in late autumn, Athenians honoured Athena and Hephaistos together, and on that day the weaving of her great robe began.

sections.heading: The peplos
sections.body:
Every year, and on a grand scale every four years, Athens gave Athena a new peplos, a woven robe, at the Panathenaia. It was woven by chosen women, the ergastinai, with the help of young girls called arrhephoroi who lived for a time on the Acropolis. Its pattern showed the battle of the gods and the giants, in which Athena fought. The robe was carried up to the Acropolis in a great procession and placed on her ancient olive-wood statue.

Think about that: the city’s greatest offering to its goddess was a piece of weaving made by many hands over months. Craft itself was worship.

sections.heading: Arachne
sections.body:
The story of Arachne, a girl who wove so well she challenged Athena, is told fully only by the Roman poet Ovid in his Metamorphoses. Arachne weaves the gods’ scandals, perfectly. Athena, angry at the insult or perhaps at being matched, destroys the tapestry and strikes the girl, who hangs herself; Athena turns her into a spider, still weaving.

It is a Roman literary tale, not Greek cult, and it can be read many ways: as a warning against pride, or as a story of an artist punished for telling the truth. Many modern devotees honour both Athena and Arachne’s skill. What is old and Greek is the core: Athena is the goddess of the loom, and she cares how well it is worked.

sections.heading: Your work as offering
sections.body:
Athena does not need perfect work. She cares for work done with attention, skill honestly learned and care. In modern devotion, people dedicate a finished piece of craft, a completed essay, a fixed engine or a well-cooked meal to her. Spinning, knitting, sewing and weaving are especially fitting, but any skill counts.

Try saying a few words to her before you begin a task: “Ergane, guide my hands.” Then give it your full attention.

knowAndDont.known: Athena Ergane is well attested in Athenian inscriptions and dedications. The Panathenaic peplos, the ergastinai and the arrhephoroi are described in ancient sources and shown on the Parthenon frieze. The Chalkeia is attested for Athens.
knowAndDont.unknown: The exact process of weaving the peplos, and how the yearly and four-yearly robes differed, is debated. Arachne has no known Greek cult and her story before Ovid is barely attested.

lessons.inPractice: Choose a craft or skill and give it fifteen minutes a day in her name this month. Some devotees weave a small band or knit a square for her shrine, replacing it each year at the Panathenaia.
reflect: What skill do you most want to grow? What would doing it well, for her, look like?
How do you feel about Arachne’s story?
further: Jenifer Neils (ed.), Goddess and Polis: The Panathenaic Festival in Ancient Athens (1992)
Joan Breton Connelly, The Parthenon Enigma (2014)

lessons.title: Promachos: war, counsel and justice
lessons.summary: The warrior goddess, the aegis, Odysseus, the court of the Areopagus, and the Medusa question.

sections.heading: The front-line fighter
sections.body:
A short Homeric hymn (number 11) is blunt: “Dread is she, and with Ares she loves deeds of war, the sack of cities and the shouting and the battle. It is she who saves the people as they go out to war and come back.” Athena Promachos, “who fights in front,” stood as a great bronze statue on the Acropolis. Victory, Nike, was her companion.

In the Iliad she fights fiercely for the Greeks. Yet she is always shown beating Ares. She guides Diomedes to wound him, and later knocks Ares down with a boulder. The Greeks saw the difference clearly: Ares is the madness of slaughter; Athena is skill, timing, courage and the protection of the people.

sections.heading: The aegis and the Gorgon
sections.body:
She wears the aegis, a goatskin cape or shield fringed with snakes, with the head of the Gorgon Medusa at its centre, the gorgoneion. It was a protective emblem, set on shields, buildings and doors to turn away harm.

Medusa’s story needs care. In Hesiod, she is simply one of three Gorgon sisters, a monster from birth; Perseus kills her with Athena’s help and gives the head to Athena. The version in which Medusa was a beautiful woman raped by Poseidon in Athena’s temple and then punished by Athena comes from Ovid, a Roman poet writing around 8 CE. Many modern people, especially survivors, have reclaimed Medusa as a symbol of protection. You can honour that and still know the history.

sections.heading: Odysseus and metis
sections.body:
Athena loved Odysseus because he was like her: quick-witted, patient, a liar when he had to be. In the Odyssey she comes to him in disguise, laughs at his inventions, and guides his son Telemachus. She is the goddess of clever survival, of thinking your way through danger.

This is a good pattern for devotion. Ask her not to fight for you but to help you think, plan and act well.

sections.heading: The court
sections.body:
In Aeschylus’ Eumenides (458 BCE), Orestes, who has killed his mother to avenge his father, flees to Athens, pursued by the Furies. Athena sets up a court of Athenian citizens on the hill of Ares, the Areopagus, to judge him. The votes are tied, and Athena casts hers for acquittal, saying she favours the male in all things since she had no mother. Then she persuades the Furies to accept a new home and honour in Athens, turning vengeance into justice.

The play founds law in place of blood feud, and it also contains her troubling vote. Both are part of how Athens imagined her: a goddess of reasoned justice, and a goddess of a male-ruled city.

knowAndDont.known: Homeric Hymn XI, the Iliad (books 5 and 21) and the Odyssey show her as warrior and guide. Hesiod (Theogony 270–283) gives the older Medusa. Ovid (Metamorphoses 4.794–803) gives the rape story. Aeschylus’ Eumenides founds the Areopagus court.
knowAndDont.unknown: We do not know how widely Ovid’s Medusa version was told before him; it may draw on lost sources, but there is no clear earlier Greek evidence. How Athenian women felt about Athena’s vote in the Eumenides is unknown.

lessons.inPractice: Devotees today often ask Athena Promachos for courage and protection, and Athena Boulaia for good counsel before decisions. A gorgoneion image by the door is a traditional protective emblem many revive. Prayers for protection ask her to guard and to give clear thinking, not to harm others.
reflect: What is the difference, for you, between Athena’s war and Ares’?
How do you hold Athena’s vote, and Medusa’s two stories?

lessons.title: Polias: the goddess of the city
lessons.summary: The contest with Poseidon, the Acropolis, the Panathenaia and the Plynteria, and Rome’s Minerva.

sections.heading: The olive and the spring
sections.body:
Athenians said that Athena and Poseidon competed for their city. Poseidon struck the rock of the Acropolis with his trident and a salt spring burst out. Athena planted an olive tree. The olive won. Visitors in ancient times were shown both the salt spring and the sacred olive tree in the Erechtheion, and when the Persians burned the Acropolis in 480 BCE, Herodotus says the olive sent up a new shoot the very next day.

Olive oil was the wealth of Attica and the prize at her games: winners at the Panathenaia received great painted amphorae of oil from her sacred trees.

sections.heading: The Acropolis
sections.body:
On the Acropolis stood her oldest image, a statue of olive wood said to have fallen from heaven, kept in the temple of Athena Polias, the city guardian. The Parthenon, built in the 440s and 430s BCE, held Pheidias’ huge gold and ivory statue of Athena Parthenos, the maiden, with Nike in her hand. In the open stood the bronze Promachos.

So Athenians honoured several Athenas on one hill. When you pray, the epithet tells her which face you are turning to.

sections.heading: Panathenaia and Plynteria
sections.body:
The Panathenaia, her birthday festival on the twenty-eighth of the month Hekatombaion in midsummer, was Athens’ greatest festival, with a procession, the new peplos, a great sacrifice and games. Every fourth year it was the Great Panathenaia, with contests in music, poetry and athletics.

In late spring came the Plynteria, “washing.” The old olive-wood statue was taken down to the sea, her robes washed and her image cleaned. It was an ill-omened day, apophras, when temples were roped off and important business avoided. Before it came the Kallynteria, the sweeping of her temple. The third of each month was her monthly day.

sections.heading: Minerva
sections.body: Rome honoured Minerva, an Italian goddess identified with Athena, as one of the three great gods of the Capitol with Jupiter and Juno. Her festival, the Quinquatria in March, was kept by craftspeople, doctors, teachers and students, who honoured her and dedicated their work. Roman polytheists today keep it. Hellenists keep the Greek forms; many people honour both.

sections.heading: Owls and the olive on your shelf
sections.body:
Athens stamped her owl on its silver coins, the “owls” that paid for the city’s fleet, and her olive branch beside it. The little owl, Athene noctua, still carries her name in its scientific Latin. Neither animal was worshipped; both were her signs, the way a seal marks a letter.

For a home shrine this is easy to borrow. An owl figure, an olive sprig or a small jar of olives, and a cup of good oil are enough to say whose shrine it is. Many people keep a little olive tree in a pot by a sunny window as a living offering, watering it on her third day. If it thrives, so much the better; if it struggles, learning to tend it properly is very much her kind of work.

knowAndDont.known: The contest with Poseidon, the olive and the salt spring are reported by Herodotus (8.55) and Pausanias (1.26–27). The Panathenaia, Plynteria and Kallynteria are well attested in Athenian sources. Panathenaic prize amphorae survive in museums.
knowAndDont.unknown: The details of the Plynteria rites, such as whether the statue was carried to the sea, are debated. Exactly how the different Athenas of the Acropolis were related in worshippers’ minds is unclear.

lessons.inPractice: Hellenists keep the Panathenaia with olive oil, honey cakes, a woven offering and a reading, and the Plynteria by cleaning their shrine and washing her image or cloth, quietly, without other business. The third of each month is her small monthly day.
reflect: What community, city or group do you want Athena to guard?
What would it mean to clean and renew your shrine as Athenians cleaned her statue?
further: Robert Parker, Polytheism and Society at Athens (2005)

practices.title: Set up her shrine
practices.instructions: Set up an orderly shrine: a candle or oil lamp, a small cup of olive oil, a dish, an owl or olive image, and a tool of your craft or a book you are studying.
practices.prompt: How does her shrine change the room?

practices.title: Read her hymns
practices.instructions: Read Homeric Hymns 11 and 28 to Athena aloud, by her shrine.
practices.prompt: Which epithet in the hymns spoke to you?

stages.title: Nine days of good work
stages.intro: Nine days of work dedicated to her, then a lesson on her days, offerings and modern devotion.

lessons.title: Her days, her offerings and her names
lessons.summary: The third of the month, the festival year, what to give, how to pray and the communities that honour her.

sections.heading: The third day and the year
sections.body:
The third day of each month, counted from the Noumenia, was Athena’s birthday in the monthly calendar, sometimes called tritomenis. Her great yearly festival is the Panathenaia in midsummer; the Plynteria falls in late spring. The app marks the Noumenia, Plynteria and Panathenaia.

A practical rhythm: on the third of each month, give oil and incense and show her your work. At the Plynteria, clean and renew the shrine in silence. At the Panathenaia, make a larger offering: a finished piece of craft, a woven band, a public act of service to your community.

sections.heading: What to give
sections.body:
Olive oil is her offering above all, poured as a libation or burned in a lamp. Olives, honey cakes, barley, incense and wine are fitting. Woven and handmade things, finished work, books, and study done in her name all count. As an Olympian goddess, her food offerings can be shared after the rite.

The Roman writer Varro, in his book on farming (37 BCE), says goats were not driven onto the Athenian Acropolis except once a year for a necessary sacrifice, so that no goat would touch the sacred olive; farmers believed a goat’s bite made an olive barren. It is a nice reminder: give her things that grow her olive, not things that harm it.

sections.heading: Names for prayer
sections.body:
Good titles are Pallas; Glaukopis, bright-eyed or owl-eyed; Parthenos, the maiden; Polias, of the city; Ergane, the worker; Promachos, front-line fighter; Nike, victory; Boulaia, of the council; Pronoia, forethought; Hygieia, health, an Acropolis title; Hippia, of horses; and Soteira, saviour.

Shape your prayer the Greek way: name her with the titles that fit, remind her of what you have given (“if ever I have poured you oil…”), and ask clearly. Ask Ergane for skill, Boulaia for good counsel, Promachos for courage, Polias for the safety of your community.

sections.heading: Who honours her now
sections.body:
Hellenic polytheists honour Athena on the third, at the Panathenaia and Plynteria, and in daily prayer for wisdom and protection. Roman polytheists honour Minerva at the Quinquatria. Many students, teachers, scholars, makers and lawyers honour her without belonging to any tradition, and eclectic Pagans often see her as a goddess of strategy and independence.

One caution: Athena has been used as a symbol by many causes, including nationalist movements. She is a goddess of her worshippers’ cities, and today she can be a guardian of any community you belong to. Devotion to her need not be about any one nation.

knowAndDont.known: The third of the month, the Panathenaia and the Plynteria are well attested. Her epithets above appear in Homer, inscriptions and Pausanias. Olive oil was central to her cult.
knowAndDont.unknown: The goat ban on the Acropolis is reported by Varro (On Agriculture 1.2.19–20), a Roman writing centuries after classical Athens; we do not know how old the rule was, or which yearly sacrifice was the exception. Modern prayers to her draw on the ancient pattern but are new.

lessons.inPractice: Mark the next Noumenia and count three days for her monthly day. Plan what you will offer at the Panathenaia or Plynteria, whichever comes next.
reflect: Which of her names describes what you most need from her?
What community will you ask her to guard?
further: Jon D. Mikalson, The Sacred and Civil Calendar of the Athenian Year (1975)

practices.title: Nine days of good work
practices.instructions: For nine days, before you begin your chosen work, wash your hands, light her candle and say a short word: “Ergane, guide my hands,” or “Pallas, clear my mind.” Then give the work at least twenty minutes of full attention. When you finish, put out the flame and note one thing you did well and one thing to improve.
practices.prompt: What did you do well today? What will you do better tomorrow?

stages.title: Counsel
stages.intro:
Athena Boulaia gives counsel. Take a few days to take counsel with yourself about the month.

Stopping here is a good outcome. So is honouring her on the third without dedicating, or finding that Hephaistos, Apollo, Hermes or another god fits better. Clear judgement, even when it says no, is exactly what she values.

practices.title: Hold a council
practices.instructions: Write down the case for dedicating and the case against, as fairly as if you were a judge on the Areopagus. Then put them away for a day and read them again.
practices.prompt: After a day, which case was stronger?

questions: Am I drawn to Athena herself, or to an image of being clever and in control?
Have I met all of her this month, including the warrior and the goddess of the Eumenides? Can I live with her hard edges?
Can I keep her third day and offer my work to her for a year?
Does her love of skill and order support me, or would it feed my perfectionism?
If I waited, would I feel relief or loss?

stages.title: Dedication with oil and work
stages.intro:
If you have chosen to go on, make your dedication on her third day, or at the Panathenaia. Bring a finished piece of work. This is a self-dedication: your own promise. It is not an initiation and makes you no priestess. Groups that initiate have their own rites, and this does not replace them.

The Athenians gave her a robe made by many hands. You give her what your own hands have made.

rite.title: Self-dedication to Athena
rite.summary: Purify, begin with Hestia, call Athena by her titles, pour olive oil, present finished work, make your promise and close in order.

ingredients.name: A bowl of fresh water and a match for khernips
Olive oil in a small cup
A finished piece of your work: craft, writing, study notes, a mended thing
A woven band, ribbon or small piece of cloth

rite.preparation: Clean the shrine and the room carefully. Finish the work you chose. Write your promise in clear words: for example, to keep her third day, to do your work with care, to give fair counsel, to defend those who need it, and to keep learning. Wash and dress neatly.

steps.title: Purify
steps.instructions: Make khernips, wash your hands and face, and sprinkle the work.

steps.title: Begin with Hestia
steps.instructions: Light the lamp and let a drop of oil fall for Hestia.
steps.spoken: Hestia, first and last: I begin with you.

steps.title: Call Athena
steps.instructions: Light incense if you have it. Stand, raise your hands.
steps.spoken: Pallas Athena, bright-eyed, Parthenos, Ergane the worker, Polias guardian of the city, Promachos, Boulaia of good counsel: if ever I have poured you oil and brought you my work, hear me. I come with a promise.

steps.title: Present the work
steps.instructions: Set your finished work before her. Tell her what it is, what it took and what you learned. Lay the woven band on the shrine if you have one.

steps.title: Make your promise
steps.instructions: Read your promise aloud. Pour most of the oil into the dish and set the olives or cake before her.
steps.spoken: This I promise, freely and with a clear mind. Guide my hands and my judgement as I keep it.

steps.title: Close with Hestia
steps.instructions: Let the last drop fall for Hestia, thank them both, and put out the flame.
steps.spoken: Hestia, last as you were first. Athena, thank you.

rite.closing: You may eat the olives or cake afterwards, as Olympian feasts were shared. Dispose of oil on earth or a cloth, not the sink. Keep the woven band on her shrine and replace it each Panathenaia. Write down your promise and what you felt.
rite.safety: Never leave an oil lamp or candle unattended; keep spilled oil away from the flame. Use a stable, heatproof surface. Incense sparingly, with a window open.

stages.title: Keeping the work
stages.intro:
Your devotion now lives in your work and in the month. Keep her third day with oil and work. Clean and renew the shrine at the Plynteria. Make a larger offering at the Panathenaia. Ask her counsel before decisions, and her skill before work.

Once a year, at the Panathenaia or on the third nearest your dedication, renew your promise, change it or set it down with thanks. If you drift, pour a little oil and start a piece of work in her name. She is patient with anyone who keeps learning.

practices.title: Her monthly third
practices.instructions: On the third day of each lunar month, give olive oil and show her what you have been working on.
practices.prompt: What did you make or learn this month?

practices.title: Plynteria and Panathenaia
practices.instructions: Clean and renew her shrine in quiet at the Plynteria; make a larger offering of work at the Panathenaia.

practices.title: Yearly rededication
practices.instructions: Repeat the dedication rite at the Panathenaia or the third nearest your dedication.
practices.prompt: What has a year of work with Athena made of you?
